title: Lazy Acres Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lazy Acres wells have a 230 ft median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $21,000-$35,000.
h1: What Wells Are Like in Lazy Acres, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land in Lazy Acres means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well depths, and water supplies that can change from one lot to the next. Permitted wells within five miles show a 230-foot median depth and a 7.0-gpm median reported yield, but those figures are only a starting point for a specific property.

Most permits identify fractured bedrock rather than a named basin aquifer. That makes nearby well records especially useful. Sunshine, Altona, Crisman, Pine Brook Hill, Seven Hills, and Jamestown can provide local comparison points, but a neighboring result is not a guarantee for a new hole.

sections.heading: Lazy Acres well depth reflects fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth around Lazy Acres is 230 feet. The middle half runs from 65 to 400 feet, meaning a driller bidding a normal residential well should allow for a broad range rather than treating 230 feet as a fixed target. The 90th-percentile depth is 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 4,550 feet.

The depth mix tells the same story: 30% of wells are under 100 feet, 29% are 100 to 300 feet, 30% are 300 to 600 feet, and 11% exceed 600 feet. Most permits name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. Granite and gneiss fractures control where water is found, so two nearby lots can require very different drilling plans.

sections.heading: Expected well yield for a Lazy Acres home
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 5.0 to 10.0 gpm, and 69% report between 5 and 15 gpm. Another 11% report more than 15 gpm, while 17% fall between 1 and 5 gpm and 2% are under 1 gpm.

For a buyer, a 7.0-gpm result is a useful working reference, not a promise. A 2% share under 1 gpm shows that very low-producing wells do occur. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any permit conditions. Household-use exempt wells remain subject to their allowed uses and the applicable pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels in Lazy Acres vary by measurement era
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a 41-foot median depth to water, with the middle half from 10 to 100 feet below the surface. That range matters for pump setting, electrical planning, and estimating how much standing water may be available in the casing.

The decade series does not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 34 feet in the 1960s, 36 feet in the 1970s, 72 feet in the 1980s, 80 feet in the 2010s, and 58 feet in the 2020s. Only 127 records report a static water level, so treat the series as local historical context rather than proof of a basin-wide trend. Seasonal conditions, elevation, fracture connections, and measurement timing can all affect a result.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers serving the area
sections.html:
The records include 4,085 permitted wells within five miles, with 2,735 recorded as constructed. Of those records, 2,869 report a total depth, 918 report a pump yield, and 127 report a static water level. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is not only an old mining or homestead dataset.

Permit activity was highest in the 1970s, with 874 permits. The records identify Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.) most often, with 816 wells, followed by Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) with 205 and Walton, with 195. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the exact scope of a bid before selecting a driller.

sections.heading: What a new well costs near Lazy Acres
sections.html:
Lazy Acres drilling is priced for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 230-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $15,000 to $23,000.

A finished residential well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, models to about $21,000 to $35,000 at that median depth. A bid can move outside that range when the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the water system needs additional treatment or storage. Have the contractor state what is included and what happens if the well is low-producing or unsuccessful.

sections.heading: Checks for water quality, septic, and a buildable lot
sections.html:
Yield is not the only risk. The mapped area within about ten miles includes 91 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 596 historic mine features, and 65 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but they are a reason to test an existing well and review nearby land uses, mine history, and water-quality records before closing.

Ask about dry-hole terms, low-yield remedies, casing and grout, pump setting, and the required water-quality panel. A septic system also needs suitable soil, setbacks, a reserve area, and room for construction equipment. Confirm the building envelope, driveway access, electrical route, and well-septic separation with the county and qualified contractors. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be relevant; verify the permit's allowed use before relying on the water.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Lazy Acres lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's own permit and construction records, then compare wells in Sunshine, Altona, Crisman, Pine Brook Hill, Seven Hills, and Jamestown. Look for depth, reported yield, static level, completion details, and the age of the pump. The broader record is useful for estimating risk, but fractured rock does not distribute water evenly.

For an existing home, obtain a current production check and water test rather than relying on a seller's description. For vacant land, make the well contingency specific: access for a rig, target depth, testing method, acceptable yield, and responsibility for a dry or low-yield hole. Price the full water system and septic work together. DWR permit review, site access, and a local driller's opinion should all be part of the purchase decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lazy Acres?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Lazy Acres is 230 feet. The middle half runs from 65 to 400 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 600 feet. Records range as deep as 4,550 feet. Because most permits name fractured bedrock, a nearby well is useful evidence but cannot predict the exact depth on a different lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Lazy Acres?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate in Lazy Acres is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 230-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $15,000 to $23,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is about $21,000 to $35,000. Bedrock conditions, access, depth, and low-yield provisions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well make in Lazy Acres?
faq.a: The median reported yield near Lazy Acres is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 10.0 gpm. Most reported wells, 69%, produce between 5 and 15 gpm. However, 2% report under 1 gpm, so buyers should review the actual well test and storage setup instead of relying only on the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Lazy Acres?
faq.a: The available well records do not prove that any individual well is safe to drink. About ten miles around Lazy Acres contain 91 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 596 historic mine features, and 65 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property's water through a qualified laboratory, review nearby land uses, and retest when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are Lazy Acres wells in the Denver Basin aquifer?
faq.a: No permitted wells in the supplied records are identified as Denver Basin aquifer wells. Most, 3,853, are assigned to an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Only 21 are listed as Alluvial and 10 as Quaternary Alluvium. Review the actual permit for allowed uses, because an exempt household-use well is not automatically a source for unrestricted irrigation or other uses.
